newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia's Chiluba rejects Mandela call to delay vote.
newsitem.headline: Zambia's Chiluba rejects Mandela call to delay vote.

text.p: Zambian President Frederick Chiluba rejected on Friday an appeal by South Africa's Nelson Mandela to postpone presidential and parliamentary elections which the opposition intends to boycott.
Chiluba's aides accused Mandela of treating Zambians like children.

Mandela intervened on Thursday, publicly calling for a postponement of the November 18 polls in the interests of peace after seven opposition parties called a boycott of what they said were rigged elections.
"I received a fax message from Mr Mandela urging me to postpone the election but that is not legally possible," Chiluba said on a campaign walkabout in the capital Lusaka.

Veteran ex-president Kenneth Kaunda has been barred from standing and his United National Independence Party (UNIP), the main opposition, is boycotting the poll in which voter cards have only reached a quarter of the 4.6 million eligible.
Chiluba replied to Mandela on Friday, saying a postponement was a "totally impossible proposal".

"Above all there is no threat to internal stability and security to warrant a draconian move like a state of emergency," Chiluba wrote in his letter. "We wish to assure you the elections will proceed peacefully."
Mandela had urged him to call off the elections -- if legally necessary by declaring a state of emergency -- and to reopen talks with his opponents.
Rioting students in Lusaka this week joined calls for renewed political dialogue. Kaunda has called for a campaign of civil disobedience but pledged it would be peaceful.
UNIP and smaller parties complain of voter registration irregularities but mostly about a new constitution passed in May, barring Kaunda and others from running for president.
The new law ruled Kaunda out because his parents were born abroad and because he had ruled for more than two terms.
A late appeal by opposition parties, who said Chiluba had lied about his own parents' background, failed to stop the poll.
Chiluba won Zambia's first free elections in 1991, putting an end to three decades of one-party rule by Kaunda.
Political analysts say Chiluba was likely to have won the elections even if Kaunda had been allowed to contest them.

Bad as life may be for ordinary Zambians in the copper-rich country, most still remember far harder times under Kaunda who ruled since independence from Britain until he gave in to pressure for free elections in 1991.
Foreign donors have frozen aid to Zambia in protest at the rising political tensions.
